chapter: Glen Island, early records and Duke Ellington
title: The 1972 argument with Ellington about emotion in music
summary: Barnet recalls a spirited dressing-room discussion at the Grove where Duke said music has no place for emotion and Barnet disagreed, citing Paul Gonsalves at Newport.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: Again to skip some time, something I've wanted to ask you for a long time, and that is about that night at the Grove in Los Angeles, I think it was 1972, when in his dressing room you and he got into a big discussion about emotion in music.

And which that poor, dear man, Bill Struthers, thought he had recorded, Bill Struthers being a disc jockey on KPFK here, and it turned out that it wasn't recorded, which is another funny story. But do you feel that Duke believed where he was arguing from that night? Because Duke took the standpoint that --
That there was no place for emotion in music.

Right. And you said that not only did you absolutely disagree with him, but that you could not believe that he felt that way from listefning to Ellington music. And it went on from there and it got to be a very heated argument.
Well, it wasn't really that. It was
never to the point of ill feelings or anything like that.
No, but there were raised voices. But do you believe that Duke believed what he was saying, or do you think that Duke was merely being a provocateur?

No, I believe that he -- at that point in his life, I believe that he really believed what he was saying. Now, there may have been a question of semantics, semantics involved there. Because as I recall I agreed with him on this point. I said a person that gets overly emotional and gets high, I mean, and really thinks he's blowing up a storm probably isn't.

Now, I went that way. But I said, 'When you say that there is no emotion at all, should be no emotion whatsoever in music,' I said, 'I have to disagree with you.' And then he started citing the symphonies, how there's -- and I said, 'Well, there again, those things have to be played a certain way and they're played the same way every time, and you can't tell me that a person, even in a symphony, doesn't feel better one night than maybe on some other night.' Where it wouldn't be evidence, you know, of any histrionics in his playing, but possibly the conductor or the people he plays with would notice it. Maybe he was more or less inspired. And I said, 'With your own band,' I said, 'The greatest example of it in the world.' I said, 'What happened with Paul

Newport. And the whole band. I said, "You can't tell me that the emotion didn't raise that band." "Oh," he said -- in other words, it wasn't so much an argument as I think possibly Duke was disapproving of people that get loaded or get high on something and go on to play and think that they're helping their playing and --
